cards.mean: with all one's effort and energy
cards.lit: staking one's life on it (the older form meant staking one's life on one piece of land)

story.text: The older form is issho kenmei, 'staking one's life on one place'. Medieval samurai held land granted by their lord and defended that single holding with their lives. Because issho ('one place') and isshō ('a whole life') sound alike, the phrase drifted to the spelling with 'whole life', which is now the usual one for doing something with all one's effort.
story.source: Medieval (Kamakura-period) samurai land holding: the older form 一所懸命

use.how: Mostly an adverb before a verb (一生懸命働く), also 一生懸命な/一生懸命になる. Said of a person's effort, not of a result.

near.diff: 無我夢中 is being so absorbed you forget yourself; 一生懸命 is deliberate, wholehearted effort, and you can promise it in advance.

cards.cue: A new employee bows at the welcome party and promises their colleagues that they will give the job everything they have.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]は毎日[まいにち]{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}練習[れんしゅう]している。
ctx.en: My little brother practises as hard as he can every day.

ctx.s: 「{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}がんばりますので、よろしくお願[ねが]いします。」
ctx.en: "I'll do my very best, so I look forward to working with you."

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもが{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}書[か]いた手紙[てがみ]を読[よ]んで、母[はは]は泣[な]いてしまった。
ctx.en: Reading the letter her child had written with such effort, the mother burst into tears.

ctx.s: 「もう少[すこ]し{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}やってくれないと困[こま]るよ」と部長[ぶちょう]に言[い]われた。
ctx.en: My manager told me, "I need you to put a bit more effort in."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は日本語[にほんご]で{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}説明[せつめい]しようとしたが、なかなか伝[つた]わらなかった。
ctx.en: She tried her hardest to explain in Japanese, but she couldn't quite get it across.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]には負[ま]けたが、選手[せんしゅ]たちの{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}な姿[すがた]に大[おお]きな拍手[はくしゅ]が送[おく]られた。
ctx.en: They lost the match, but the players got a big round of applause for how hard they had tried.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]とは{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}の友達[ともだち]でいたい。
bad.en: (meant: I want us to be friends for life)
bad.why: Isshō alone means 'a whole lifetime'; isshōkenmei is about effort. A lifelong friend is isshō no tomodachi.

bad.s: 今回[こんかい]のテストの結果[けっか]は{一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: this time my test results were excellent)
bad.why: It describes how hard a person tries, not how good a result is. Say kekka ga totemo yokatta.

cards.mean: getting two benefits from a single action
cards.lit: one stone, two birds

story.text: Unlike most four-character idioms, this one does not come from the Chinese classics. It is a Japanese rendering of the English proverb 'to kill two birds with one stone', put into the four-character form and now used as an ordinary Japanese idiom.
story.source: Translation of the English proverb 'kill two birds with one stone'

use.how: A noun: Xは一石二鳥だ, 一石二鳥の方法/アイデア. Said of a plan or action that brings two good results at once.

near.diff: 一挙両得 means the same but sounds more formal and written; 一石二鳥 is the everyday choice in conversation.

cards.cue: You start cycling to work instead of taking the train: you save on fares and get your exercise without setting extra time aside.

ctx.s: 自転車[じてんしゃ]通勤[つうきん]は運動[うんどう]にもなるし、お金[かね]も節約[せつやく]できて{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}だ。
ctx.en: Cycling to work is exercise and saves money too: two birds with one stone.

ctx.s: 「好[す]きな歌[うた]で英語[えいご]を勉強[べんきょう]すれば、楽[たの]しいし覚[おぼ]えられるし、{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}じゃない？」
ctx.en: "If you study English with songs you like, it's fun and you remember things. Isn't that two birds with one stone?"

ctx.s: 出張[しゅっちょう]のついでに実家[じっか]にも寄[よ]れて、{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}だった。
ctx.en: I could drop in on my parents while I was there on business, so it worked out doubly well.

ctx.s: 庭[にわ]で野菜[やさい]を育[そだ]てるのは、食費[しょくひ]も浮[う]くし趣味[しゅみ]にもなる{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}の方法[ほうほう]だ。
ctx.en: Growing vegetables in the garden cuts the food bill and gives you a hobby: it kills two birds with one stone.

ctx.s: 「売[う]れ残[のこ]りをまかないに使[つか]えば、ごみも減[へ]って{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}ですね」と店長[てんちょう]が言[い]った。
ctx.en: "If we use the leftovers for the staff meals, we cut waste as well. Two birds with one stone," said the manager.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい制度[せいど]は、社員[しゃいん]の健康[けんこう]と仕事[しごと]の効率[こうりつ]を同時[どうじ]に高[たか]める{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}の試[こころ]みとして注目[ちゅうもく]されている。
ctx.en: The new scheme is drawing attention as a way to improve both staff health and work efficiency at once.

bad.s: 財布[さいふ]も携帯[けいたい]もなくして、{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: I lost my wallet and my phone in one go)
bad.why: It is only for two gains from one action. Two losses at once is a different idea (nakittsura ni hachi, for instance).

bad.s: この方法[ほうほう]で、時間[じかん]とお金[かね]を{一石二鳥[いっせきにちょう]}した。
bad.en: (meant: with this method I saved both time and money)
bad.why: It is a noun and cannot take suru. Say jikan mo okane mo setsuyaku dekite isseki nichō datta.

cards.mean: every person has their own tastes and ideas
cards.lit: ten people, ten colours: each person has a colour of their own

use.how: Usually a predicate, Xは十人十色だ, or 十人十色で… Said of tastes, opinions and ways of doing things that differ from person to person.

near.diff: 千差万別 says things of any kind vary enormously; 十人十色 is specifically about people differing in taste, opinion or style.

cards.cue: Asked which ramen shop is best, five friends name five different places, and someone shrugs: that's just how people are.

ctx.s: 好[す]きな食[た]べ物[もの]は{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}だ。
ctx.en: Everyone has different favourite foods.

ctx.s: 「休[やす]みの日[ひ]の過[す]ごし方[かた]なんて、{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}でしょう。」
ctx.en: "How people spend their days off varies from person to person, doesn't it?"

ctx.s: 同[おな]じ本[ほん]を読[よ]んでも、感想[かんそう]は{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}で面白[おもしろ]い。
ctx.en: Even when people read the same book, their impressions all differ, which is interesting.

ctx.s: 子育[こそだ]てのやり方[かた]は{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}だから、よその家[いえ]と比[くら]べなくていいよ。
ctx.en: Every parent raises children their own way, so you don't need to compare yourself with other families.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]は「勉強[べんきょう]の仕方[しかた]は{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}です。自分[じぶん]に合[あ]う方法[ほうほう]を探[さが]しましょう」と言[い]った。
ctx.en: The teacher said, "Everyone studies differently. Find the method that suits you."

ctx.s: アンケートの回答[かいとう]は{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}で、一[ひと]つの意見[いけん]にまとめるのは難[むずか]しかった。
ctx.en: The survey answers were all over the place, and it was hard to sum them up as one view.

bad.s: このシャツは{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}で、色[いろ]がたくさんある。
bad.en: (meant: this shirt comes in lots of colours)
bad.why: The colours are a metaphor for people's differences. A shirt sold in many colours is iro ga hōfu da.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]は{十人十色[じゅうにんといろ]}でバーベキューをした。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday ten of us had a barbecue)
bad.why: It is not a head count. Ten people is jūnin de; jūnin toiro only says that people differ.

cards.mean: suffering the results of one's own bad actions
cards.lit: one's own deeds, one's own receiving

story.text: A Buddhist term. Gō is karma, the deeds a person does, and toku is receiving. The teaching is that the fruits of your actions, good or bad, return to you yourself. In everyday Japanese only the bad half remains: it now says that someone's trouble is the result of their own conduct.

use.how: A predicate: それは自業自得だ. Said of trouble a person brought on themselves, often bluntly about others, or wryly about oneself.

near.diff: 因果応報 states a moral law that covers good and bad deeds alike; 自業自得 is the blunt verdict that someone's own fault caused their trouble.

cards.cue: Your brother played games all week instead of revising, failed the test, and now wants your sympathy. You have none.

ctx.s: 夜更[よふ]かしして寝坊[ねぼう]したのは{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だ。
ctx.en: Oversleeping after staying up late is your own fault.

ctx.s: 「テスト前[まえ]に遊[あそ]んでばかりいたんだから、{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "You did nothing but play before the test, so you brought it on yourself."

ctx.s: 飲[の]みすぎて二日酔[ふつかよ]いになったけど、{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だから文句[もんく]は言[い]えない。
ctx.en: I drank too much and have a hangover, but it's my own doing, so I can't complain.

ctx.s: スピード違反[いはん]で捕[つか]まった兄[あに]に、父[ちち]は「{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だ」とだけ言[い]った。
ctx.en: When my brother was caught speeding, all my father said was, "You asked for it."

ctx.s: 嘘[うそ]を重[かさ]ねて信用[しんよう]を失[うしな]ったのは、まさに{自業自得[じごうじとく]}と言[い]える。
ctx.en: Losing people's trust after telling lie after lie is exactly what one deserves.

ctx.s: 「確[たし]かに{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だけど、少[すこ]しかわいそうな気[き]もするね。」
ctx.en: "Sure, he brought it on himself, but I feel a bit sorry for him."

bad.s: 毎日[まいにち]練習[れんしゅう]したから優勝[ゆうしょう]できた。{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: I practised every day and won, so I earned it)
bad.why: In modern Japanese it is only for bad results. For a success you earned, say doryoku ga minotta.

bad.s: 地震[じしん]で家[いえ]が壊[こわ]れてしまったのは{自業自得[じごうじとく]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: it was terrible luck that the earthquake destroyed the house)
bad.why: It blames the person for their own conduct. Used about an innocent victim it sounds cruel, not sympathetic.

cards.mean: every encounter happens only once, so treasure it
cards.lit: one lifetime, one meeting

story.text: A phrase from the tea ceremony. Yamanoue Sōji, a pupil of the tea master Sen no Rikyū, wrote that from entering the tea garden until leaving, a guest should behave as if the gathering came only once in a lifetime. In the nineteenth century Ii Naosuke set the idea down as ichigo ichie in his writing on tea: host and guest should give the gathering their full sincerity, because it will never happen again in the same way.
story.source: Tea ceremony: 『山上宗二記』 and 井伊直弼『茶湯一会集』

use.how: A noun: 一期一会の出会い, 一期一会を大切にする. Said about meetings with people, and the attitude of treasuring each one.

near.diff: 千載一遇 is a rare chance or opportunity; 一期一会 is about a meeting between people that will not be repeated.

cards.cue: On a trip you talk for hours with a stranger in a café, know you'll never see them again, and feel the meeting was precious.

ctx.s: 旅先[たびさき]での出会[であ]いは{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}だ。
ctx.en: Encounters on a journey happen only once.

ctx.s: 「一度[いちど]しか会[あ]わなかったけど、あれは{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}の出会[であ]いだったと思[おも]う。」
ctx.en: "We only met once, but I think it was one of those meetings you treasure for life."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]の口癖[くちぐせ]は「人[ひと]との縁[えん]は{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}」だった。
ctx.en: My grandmother always used to say, "Every meeting with a person happens only once."

ctx.s: {一期一会[いちごいちえ]}を大切[たいせつ]にしたいので、どのお客様[きゃくさま]にも心[こころ]を込[こ]めて接[せっ]しています。
ctx.en: I want to treasure each encounter, so I put my heart into serving every customer.

ctx.s: このメンバーで演奏[えんそう]できるのは今夜[こんや]だけ。まさに{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}のステージだ。
ctx.en: Tonight is the only time this line-up will ever play together: a one-time-only stage in the truest sense.

ctx.s: 茶道[さどう]では、客[きゃく]をもてなす心構[こころがま]えとして{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}が説[と]かれる。
ctx.en: In the tea ceremony, treating each gathering as unrepeatable is taught as the proper spirit of hospitality.

bad.s: 株[かぶ]が安[やす]い今[いま]は{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}のチャンスだ。
bad.en: (meant: with shares this cheap, now is a once-in-a-lifetime chance)
bad.why: It is about meetings between people, not opportunities. A rare chance is senzai ichigū no chansu.

bad.s: 旅行中[りょこうちゅう]に素敵[すてき]な人[ひと]と{一期一会[いちごいちえ]}した。
bad.en: (meant: on my trip I happened to meet a lovely person)
bad.why: It is a noun and cannot take suru. Say ichigo ichie no deai ga atta.

cards.mean: all day long, all the time
cards.lit: throughout four times six hours: the whole twenty-four-hour day

story.text: In the old Japanese system the day was divided into twelve periods, so 'all day and night' was nirokujichū, two times six. After the twenty-four-hour clock came into use, the phrase was remade as shirokujichū, four times six, and the new form replaced the old one.
story.source: The older form 二六時中, from the twelve-period day

use.how: An adverb before the verb: 四六時中スマホを見ている. Says something goes on constantly, often with mild exaggeration or complaint. Casual rather than formal.

near.diff: 一日中 covers one particular whole day (昨日は一日中寝ていた); 四六時中 says something happens constantly, day after day.

cards.cue: Your teenage son seems to have his phone in his hand from the moment he wakes until he sleeps, every single day, even at dinner.

ctx.s: うちの猫[ねこ]は{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}寝[ね]ている。
ctx.en: Our cat sleeps pretty much all the time.

ctx.s: 「{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}スマホばかり見[み]ていないで、少[すこ]しは外[そと]に出[で]なさい。」
ctx.en: "Stop staring at your phone all day long and get outside for a bit."

ctx.s: 「あの二人[ふたり]、{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}一緒[いっしょ]にいるね。」
ctx.en: "Those two are together every minute of the day, aren't they?"

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]が近[ちか]いので、{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}そのことが頭[あたま]から離[はな]れない。
ctx.en: The exam is close, so I can't get it out of my head for a moment.

ctx.s: 駅前[えきまえ]のコンビニは、{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}人[ひと]が出入[でい]りしている。
ctx.en: People are going in and out of the convenience store by the station around the clock.

ctx.s: 赤[あか]ちゃんが生[う]まれてからは、{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}誰[だれ]かがそばにいなければならなくなった。
ctx.en: Since the baby was born, someone has to be with it at all hours.

bad.s: {四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}お世話[せわ]になっております。
bad.en: (meant: thank you for your continued support, in a business email)
bad.why: It sounds casual and suggests something relentless. The fixed business greeting is itsumo osewa ni natte orimasu.

bad.s: この薬[くすり]は{四六時中[しろくじちゅう]}ごとに一回[いっかい]飲[の]んでください。
bad.en: (meant: take this medicine once every twenty-four hours)
bad.why: It is an adverb meaning 'constantly', not a unit of time. Once a day is ichinichi ikkai.

cards.mean: obvious at a single glance
cards.lit: one look, and it is clear

use.how: A predicate: 違いは一目瞭然だ, or 一目瞭然になる. Said of a fact, difference or result that anyone can see the moment they look.

cards.cue: Once the monthly sales are drawn as a bar chart, anyone looking at it can see instantly which month was the worst.

ctx.en: Put it in a graph and the difference is obvious at a glance.

ctx.s: 「どっちが勝[か]ったかなんて、写真[しゃしん]を見[み]れば{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}でしょう。」
ctx.en: "Just look at the photo and you can see straight away who won."

ctx.s: 散[ち]らかった部屋[へや]を見[み]れば、彼[かれ]が忙[いそが]しかったことは{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}だった。
ctx.en: One look at his messy room made it obvious he'd been busy.

ctx.s: 色分[いろわ]けしておけば、どの書類[しょるい]がどこにあるか{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}になる。
ctx.en: If you colour-code them, you can see at once which papers are where.

ctx.s: このアプリなら、今月[こんげつ]いくら使[つか]ったかが{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}だ。
ctx.en: With this app you can see at a glance how much you've spent this month.

ctx.s: 点検[てんけん]結果[けっか]は表[ひょう]にまとめ、問題[もんだい]のある箇所[かしょ]が{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}となるようにした。
ctx.en: The inspection results were put in a table so that the problem areas stand out immediately.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は裏表[うらおもて]がなくて{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}な人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is an open, straightforward person)
bad.why: It says a fact or difference is plain to see, not that a person is frank. Say uraomote no nai hito.

bad.s: 地図[ちず]を見[み]て、駅[えき]までの道[みち]を{一目瞭然[いちもくりょうぜん]}した。
bad.en: (meant: I looked at the map and understood the way to the station at once)
bad.why: It is not a verb and cannot take suru. Say chizu o mireba michi wa ichimoku ryōzen datta.

cards.mean: finding a way by trial and error
cards.lit: trying, and getting it wrong, and trying again

use.how: A noun that also takes する: 試行錯誤する, 試行錯誤を重ねる, 試行錯誤の末に. Said of repeatedly trying methods until one works.

near.diff: 四苦八苦 is struggling painfully with something hard; 試行錯誤 is the method of trying again and again and learning from each failure.

cards.cue: A baker spends weeks changing the flour, the water and the oven time with each batch until the bread finally comes out right.

ctx.s: {試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}しながら、新[あたら]しい料理[りょうり]を作[つく]ってみた。
ctx.en: I made a new dish, working it out by trial and error.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]も{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}を重[かさ]ねて、やっと理想[りそう]の味[あじ]になった。
ctx.en: After trying again and again, I finally got the flavour I wanted.

ctx.s: 「最初[さいしょ]からうまくいく人[ひと]なんていないよ。みんな{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}してるんだから。」
ctx.en: "Nobody gets it right first time. Everyone finds their way by trial and error."

ctx.s: 「この棚[たな]、どうやって組[く]み立[た]てたの？」「説明書[せつめいしょ]がなかったから、{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "How did you put this shelf together?" "There were no instructions, so it was trial and error."

ctx.s: 開発[かいはつ]チームは試作品[しさくひん]を何十回[なんじっかい]も作[つく]り直[なお]す{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}の末[すえ]、ようやく製品[せいひん]を完成[かんせい]させた。
ctx.en: After rebuilding the prototype dozens of times by trial and error, the development team finally completed the product.

ctx.s: 教[おし]え方[かた]に正解[せいかい]はなく、今[いま]も{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}の毎日[まいにち]です。
ctx.en: There is no single right way to teach, so every day is still trial and error for me.

bad.s: 計算[けいさん]で{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}して、答[こた]えを間違[まちが]えてしまった。
bad.en: (meant: I made a mistake in my calculation and got the answer wrong)
bad.why: Sakugo here is not one slip: the idiom names a process of repeated attempts. One miscalculation is keisan misu.

bad.s: 一回目[いっかいめ]で{試行錯誤[しこうさくご]}して、すぐに成功[せいこう]した。
bad.en: (meant: I tried it once and succeeded straight away)
bad.why: It implies many attempts and failures before success, so it contradicts getting it right first time.

cards.mean: understanding each other without words
cards.lit: by the mind, passing to the mind

story.text: A Zen Buddhist phrase. Zen holds that the deepest truth cannot be put fully into words or scriptures, so it is passed from master to disciple directly, mind to mind. Everyday Japanese borrowed the phrase for people who know each other so well that they understand one another without saying anything.

use.how: A noun: 以心伝心で分かる, 以心伝心の仲. Said of couples, friends or colleagues who grasp each other's thoughts without words; also of relying on that.

near.diff: 意気投合 is hitting it off, usually through talk, often on first meeting; 以心伝心 is long familiarity that makes words unnecessary.

cards.cue: Before you even open your mouth, your partner hands you exactly the thing you were about to ask for.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]連[つ]れ添[そ]った両親[りょうしん]は、{以心伝心[いしんでんしん]}で通[つう]じ合[あ]っている。
ctx.en: My parents, married for decades, understand each other without a word.

ctx.s: 「醤油[しょうゆ]取[と]って」と言[い]う前[まえ]に、夫[おっと]が渡[わた]してくれた。{以心伝心[いしんでんしん]}だ。
ctx.en: My husband passed me the soy sauce before I could ask. He read my mind.

cards.mean: the matter is settled at last

cards.mean: cornered with no way out
cards.lit: body cut off, life cut off: every way out is closed

story.text: Zettai and zetsumei are the names of two ill-omened stars in kyūsei, the nine-star divination that came to Japan from China; they signified ruin. To be under them was to face catastrophe, and the pair came to mean any situation with no escape.

near.diff: 危機一髪 stresses how narrowly a disaster was avoided; 絶体絶命 describes being trapped with no way out, before any rescue comes.

ctx.s: 資金[しきん]が尽[つ]き、会社[かいしゃ]は{絶体絶命[ぜったいぜつめい]}の窮地[きゅうち]に立[た]たされた。
ctx.en: With its funds exhausted, the company was backed into a hopeless corner.

cards.mean: praising one's own work or actions
cards.lit: one's own picture, one's own praise: writing the tribute on a painting you made

story.text: A san is a poem or line of praise inscribed on an East Asian painting, often added by someone else, such as a scholar or a monk, to honour the picture. Writing the san on a picture you painted yourself means praising your own work, and that is the image behind the phrase.
story.source: 画賛 (inscriptions on East Asian paintings)

ctx.en: "It may sound like I'm praising myself, but I'm confident in this proposal."

ctx.en: The department head is always singing the praises of their own ideas.

ctx.en: "Look at this photo. Doesn't it look professional?" "There you go, praising yourself again."

ctx.s: 作者[さくしゃ]の{自画自賛[じがじさん]}ばかりで、読者[どくしゃ]の感想[かんそう]が一[ひと]つも載[の]っていない。
ctx.en: It's all the author praising their own book; there isn't a single reader's opinion in it.

cards.mean: struggling hard to cope with something
cards.lit: four sufferings, eight sufferings

story.text: In Buddhism the four sufferings are birth, old age, sickness and death. The eight add four more: parting from those you love, meeting those you hate, not getting what you seek, and the suffering of the five aggregates that make up body and mind. Together they stand for all the pain of human life; everyday Japanese uses the phrase for a hard struggle with something.

use.how: Usually 〜に四苦八苦する or 四苦八苦して〜: a person struggling with a concrete task or problem (a jar lid, a report, money). Everyday, often wry, not for real tragedy.

near.diff: 試行錯誤 is trying method after method until one works; 四苦八苦 stresses how much trouble and strain the struggle takes.

cards.cue: You spent an hour wrestling with flat-pack furniture, instructions in a language you can't read and screws everywhere.

ctx.en: "I'm really struggling to move all my boxes on my own. Could you give me a hand?"

ctx.s: 初[はじ]めての海外生活[かいがいせいかつ]で、言葉[ことば]が通[つう]じず{四苦八苦[しくはっく]}した。

ctx.en: The staff can't work out the new system and are having a dreadful time with it.

ctx.s: 「論文[ろんぶん]、進[すす]んでる？」「英語[えいご]の要約[ようやく]に{四苦八苦[しくはっく]}してるところ。」

bad.en: (meant: he is grieving after losing his family in an accident)

cards.mean: carelessness is your worst enemy

cards.mean: adapting flexibly to the situation at hand

cards.mean: having both strong points and weak points
cards.lit: one long, one short: one point where it is strong, one where it falls short

ctx.en: Trains and cars each have pluses and minuses, so you can't say which is more convenient.

ctx.en: "Which of these two laptops do you think is better?" "Hmm, each has its good and bad points."

ctx.en: Nobody is perfect. Everyone has strengths and weaknesses.

bad.s: 日本語[にほんご]は{一長一短[いっちょういったん]}には上達[じょうたつ]しない。
bad.en: (meant: you can't get good at Japanese overnight)
bad.why: That is the look-alike icchou isseki (overnight). Icchou ittan means pros and cons and is never an expression of time.

cards.mean: rushing this way and that in confusion
cards.lit: going right, going left: running back and forth without knowing which way to go

near.diff: 東奔西走 is running around busily with a purpose; 右往左往 is milling about in confusion, getting nowhere.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は鍵[かぎ]が見[み]つからず、玄関[げんかん]の前[まえ]で{右往左往[うおうさおう]}していた。

ctx.s: 突然[とつぜん]の仕様変更[しようへんこう]に、開発[かいはつ]チームはどの方針[ほうしん]で進[すす]めればいいかわからず、{右往左往[うおうさおう]}するばかりだった。

bad.en: (meant: as a salesperson I run around visiting clients every day)

cards.r: たんとうちょくにゅう

cards.lit: a single sword, straight in: one warrior with one blade charging straight at the enemy

cards.mean: the whole story from beginning to end

bad.why: It is not a word for grief. It means alternating hope and worry as news changes, which makes no sense after a death.

cards.mean: so outrageous it is beyond words
cards.lit: the path of words is cut off

story.text: Originally a Buddhist expression: the deepest truth of the Buddha's teaching is so profound that the way of words is cut off, and it cannot be put into language. Over time the sense shifted from 'too profound for words' to 'too outrageous for words', and today it is used only to condemn.

use.how: Usually 〜など/なんて言語道断だ, or 言語道断の行為: a strong, often indignant condemnation of serious wrongdoing that cannot be excused.

near.diff: 前代未聞 only says something has never happened before; 言語道断 condemns an act as morally unacceptable.

cards.cue: A colleague suggests quietly selling customers' personal data for extra money. Your boss rejects the idea with moral outrage. What does the boss call it?

ctx.s: 飲酒[いんしゅ]運転[うんてん]なんて{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}だ。
ctx.en: Drink-driving is absolutely unacceptable.

ctx.s: 人[ひと]の作品[さくひん]を自分[じぶん]のものとして発表[はっぴょう]するなど、{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}だ。
ctx.en: Presenting someone else's work as your own is outrageous.

ctx.s: 「カンニングは{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}。見[み]つけたらその場[ば]で零点[れいてん]です」と先生[せんせい]が言[い]った。
ctx.en: "Cheating is out of the question. If I catch you, you get zero on the spot," said the teacher.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]は「顧客[こきゃく]の情報[じょうほう]を外部[がいぶ]に漏[も]らすなど{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}だ」と厳[きび]しく述[の]べた。
ctx.en: The president said sternly, "Leaking customer information outside the company is beyond words."

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもへの暴力[ぼうりょく]は、どんな理由[りゆう]があっても{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}です。
ctx.en: Violence against children is unforgivable, whatever the reason.

ctx.s: 「審判[しんぱん]に暴言[ぼうげん]を吐[は]くなど{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}の行為[こうい]だ」と、監督[かんとく]は選手[せんしゅ]を厳[きび]しく叱[しか]った。
ctx.en: "Hurling abuse at the referee is an outrageous thing to do," the coach told the player off sternly.

bad.s: この景色[けしき]は{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}の美[うつく]しさだ。
bad.en: (meant: this view is indescribably beautiful)
bad.why: In modern Japanese it only condemns. For beauty beyond words say kotoba ni dekinai hodo utsukushii.

bad.s: 「傘[かさ]を忘[わす]れたの？{言語道断[ごんごどうだん]}だよ。」
bad.en: (meant: you forgot your umbrella? how silly)
bad.why: Far too strong for a small slip. It is reserved for serious wrongdoing that deserves moral outrage.

cards.mean: putting the right person in the right job
cards.lit: the right material in the right place

use.how: As a noun or predicate (適材適所だ, 適材適所の配置/人事, 適材適所で決める): about assigning people roles that suit their abilities.

near.diff: 十人十色 just says people all differ; 適材適所 is about using those differences by giving each person the role that suits them.

cards.cue: A new manager moves the shy but meticulous salesman to quality control and the talkative engineer to customer support, and both thrive.

ctx.s: 「料理[りょうり]は兄[あに]、片付[かたづ]けは私[わたし]。{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}だね。」
ctx.en: "My brother cooks and I clear up. Everyone doing what they're good at."

ctx.s: 文化祭[ぶんかさい]では、絵[え]が得意[とくい]な人[ひと]にポスターを任[まか]せるなど、{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}で役割[やくわり]を決[き]めた。
ctx.en: For the school festival we assigned roles by strengths, for example giving the posters to people good at drawing.

ctx.s: 「彼[かれ]を営業[えいぎょう]から開発[かいはつ]に移[うつ]したのは、まさに{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}だった。」
ctx.en: "Moving him from sales to development was exactly the right call for his talents."

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい部長[ぶちょう]は、{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}の人事[じんじ]でチームを立[た]て直[なお]した。
ctx.en: The new department head turned the team around by putting each person in the right post.

ctx.s: 社員[しゃいん]一人一人[ひとりひとり]の強[つよ]みを生[い]かす{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}の配置[はいち]が大切[たいせつ]だ。
ctx.en: Placing staff so that each person's strengths are put to use is essential.

ctx.s: 「この配置[はいち]は、本当[ほんとう]に{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}と言[い]えるでしょうか。」
ctx.en: "Can we really say this arrangement puts the right people in the right roles?"

bad.s: この靴[くつ]は{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}で、足[あし]にぴったりだ。
bad.en: (meant: these shoes fit my feet perfectly)
bad.why: It is about assigning people to roles that suit them, not about something fitting well. Say pittari au.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はとても{適材適所[てきざいてきしょ]}な人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is a very capable person)
bad.why: It describes a good placement of people, not a personal quality, so it cannot describe someone as capable.

cards.mean: many people saying the same thing
cards.lit: different mouths, the same sound

use.how: Almost always 異口同音に + a verb of saying (言う, 答える, 語る): many different people giving the same opinion or answer.

near.diff: 満場一致 is a formal unanimous vote or decision; 異口同音 is many people separately saying the same words or opinion.

cards.cue: You ask five different friends about a new café, one by one, and every single one says the cakes are the best in town.

ctx.s: 店[みせ]を訪[おとず]れた客[きゃく]は、{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に「また来[き]たい」と言[い]う。
ctx.en: Everyone who visits the shop says the same thing: "I want to come back."

ctx.s: 「誰[だれ]に聞[き]いても{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に、あの先生[せんせい]の授業[じゅぎょう]はわかりやすいって言[い]うよ。」
ctx.en: "Whoever you ask, they all say that teacher's classes are easy to follow."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]が「楽[たの]しかった？」と聞[き]くと、子[こ]どもたちは{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に「楽[たの]しかった！」と答[こた]えた。
ctx.en: When the teacher asked "Did you have fun?", the children all answered together, "Yes!"

ctx.s: 試合後[しあいご]、選手[せんしゅ]たちは{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に「観客[かんきゃく]の声援[せいえん]が力[ちから]になった」と語[かた]った。
ctx.en: After the match the players all said the same thing: the crowd's support had spurred them on.

ctx.s: 目撃者[もくげきしゃ]は{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に「車[くるま]は赤信号[あかしんごう]を無視[むし]した」と証言[しょうげん]した。
ctx.en: The witnesses all testified alike that the car had run the red light.

ctx.s: 「専門家[せんもんか]が{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に危険[きけん]だと言[い]っているのに、まだ信[しん]じないの？」
ctx.en: "Every expert is saying it's dangerous, and you still don't believe it?"

bad.s: 二人[ふたり]は{異口同音[いくどうおん]}で、何[なに]も言[い]わなくても気持[きも]ちが通[つう]じる。
bad.en: (meant: the two understand each other without saying anything)
bad.why: It is about many people saying the same thing aloud. Understanding without words is ishin denshin.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は毎朝[まいあさ]、子[こ]どもに{異口同音[いくどうおん]}に同[おな]じことを言[い]う。
bad.en: (meant: every morning I tell my child the same thing over and over)
bad.why: It needs many different speakers. One person repeating themselves just says onaji koto o nando mo iu.

cards.mean: overnight (mostly: it cannot be done that fast)
cards.lit: one morning and one evening

story.text: The commentary on the hexagram Kun in the Book of Changes says that when a minister kills his lord or a son kills his father, the cause did not arise in one morning or one evening; it built up little by little. From this, 'one morning, one evening' came to mean a very short time, used above all to say that something cannot happen that fast.
story.source: 『易経』坤卦・文言伝 (Book of Changes)

use.how: Almost always negative: 一朝一夕には〜ない, 一朝一夕にできるものではない, 一朝一夕にはいかない. Said of skills, trust or results that take long to build.

near.diff: 一長一短 (いっちょういったん) only sounds similar: it means having both merits and faults, nothing to do with time.

cards.cue: A beginner asks how to become fluent in a month. You want to say it simply cannot be done that quickly.

ctx.s: 語学[ごがく]は{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}には身[み]につかない。
ctx.en: You can't pick up a language overnight.

ctx.s: 「信頼[しんらい]は{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}に築[きず]けるものじゃないよ。」
ctx.en: "Trust isn't something you can build overnight."

ctx.s: 「たった一週間[いっしゅうかん]で上手[じょうず]になりたい？{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}にはいかないよ。」
ctx.en: "You want to get good in just a week? It doesn't happen that fast."

ctx.s: 「この味[あじ]は{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}に出[だ]せるものじゃありません」と店主[てんしゅ]は笑[わら]った。
ctx.en: "This flavour isn't something you can produce overnight," the owner said with a smile.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]の赤字[あかじ]が{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}に解消[かいしょう]されるはずがない。
ctx.en: Losses built up over many years can't possibly be wiped out overnight.

ctx.s: この町[まち]の美[うつく]しい景観[けいかん]は{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}にできたものではなく、百年[ひゃくねん]かけて作[つく]られた。
ctx.en: This town's beautiful streetscape did not appear overnight; it was shaped over a hundred years.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は英語[えいご]を{一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}に覚[おぼ]えた。
bad.en: (meant: he learned English overnight)
bad.why: It is used almost only in negative statements. To say something really happened fast, use attoiu ma ni.

bad.s: {一朝一夕[いっちょういっせき]}、毎日[まいにち]ピアノの練習[れんしゅう]を続[つづ]けた。
bad.en: (meant: I practised the piano morning and evening every day)
bad.why: It means a very short time, not mornings and evenings. For practising morning and night say asaban.

cards.r: じゃくにくきょうしょく
cards.mean: the strong prey on the weak
cards.lit: the weak are meat, the strong eat

story.text: The Tang writer Han Yu, in a farewell essay for the Buddhist monk Wenchang, wrote that birds peck at their food with heads bowed and then look up and around, and beasts live deep in the wild and seldom come out, for fear of being harmed, and still they do not escape: the weak are meat, and the strong eat them.
story.source: 韓愈「送浮屠文暢師序」 (Han Yu, Tang dynasty)

use.how: 弱肉強食だ or 弱肉強食の + noun (世界, 社会, 競争): describes a world of harsh competition, in nature or in society, where the strong win and the weak are swallowed up.

near.diff: 適者生存 is the scientific 'survival of the fittest'; 弱肉強食 stresses the strong devouring the weak and is often a bitter remark about society.

cards.cue: A giant chain opens in the area, cuts prices, and within a year every small family shop nearby has closed. What kind of world is the market?

ctx.s: 自然[しぜん]の世界[せかい]は{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}だ。
ctx.en: The natural world is one where the strong eat the weak.

ctx.s: サバンナの{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}の世界[せかい]を描[えが]いたドキュメンタリーを見[み]た。
ctx.en: I watched a documentary about the kill-or-be-killed world of the savanna.

ctx.s: 「この業界[ぎょうかい]は{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}だから、小[ちい]さな会社[かいしゃ]はすぐ大手[おおて]に飲[の]み込[こ]まれる。」
ctx.en: "In this industry the strong devour the weak, so small firms are soon swallowed by the big ones."

ctx.s: 「社会[しゃかい]は{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}なんだから、甘[あま]えるな」と父[ちち]は言[い]った。
ctx.en: "Society is survival of the strongest, so don't expect to be coddled," my father said.

ctx.s: 価格[かかく]競争[きょうそう]が激[はげ]しくなり、市場[しじょう]は{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}の様相[ようそう]を呈[てい]している。
ctx.en: As price competition intensifies, the market is taking on a dog-eat-dog character.

ctx.s: {弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}の社会[しゃかい]で、弱[よわ]い立場[たちば]の人[ひと]をどう守[まも]るべきだろうか。
ctx.en: In a society where the strong prey on the weak, how should we protect people in vulnerable positions?

bad.s: うちの猫[ねこ]は魚[さかな]より肉[にく]が好[す]きで、{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: my cat prefers meat to fish)
bad.why: It is not about diet. It describes a harsh world where the strong defeat and exploit the weak.

bad.s: 強[つよ]い先輩[せんぱい]が弱[よわ]い後輩[こうはい]に優[やさ]しく教[おし]えるのは、{弱肉強食[じゃくにくきょうしょく]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: it's a good system where the strong help the weak)
bad.why: It means the opposite: the strong prey on the weak. Strong people helping the weak is not described by it.

cards.mean: the four-part structure of a story or essay
cards.lit: open, develop, turn, conclude: the four steps of a well-built piece

story.text: The term comes from the craft of classical Chinese poetry. In a four-line quatrain (jueju), each line had its job: the first opens the scene, the second develops it, the third turns to something unexpected, and the last ties everything together. In Japan the same four steps were later applied to essays, speeches and, famously, four-panel comic strips.
story.source: Classical Chinese poetics: the structure of the jueju quatrain (起承転合 in Chinese)

use.how: A noun for the structure of a story, essay, speech or comic: 起承転結がある / はっきりしている / を意識して書く. Not for the steps of a task or process.

cards.cue: A teacher tells the class that a good essay needs an opening, a development, a twist and a conclusion.

ctx.s: 作文[さくぶん]は{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}を意識[いしき]して書[か]きましょう。
ctx.en: When you write your essay, keep the opening-development-twist-conclusion structure in mind.

ctx.s: この四[よん]コマ漫画[まんが]は{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}がはっきりしていて面白[おもしろ]い。
ctx.en: This four-panel comic has a clear setup, development, twist and punchline, which makes it fun.

ctx.s: 「君[きみ]の話[はなし]は{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}の『転[てん]』がないから、盛[も]り上[あ]がらないんだよ。」
ctx.en: "Your story has no twist, so it never builds to anything."

ctx.s: 「論文[ろんぶん]でも{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}で書[か]くべきですか？」
ctx.en: "Should an academic paper also follow the four-part structure?"

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]のスピーチは{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}が見事[みごと]で、最後[さいご]に会場[かいじょう]が沸[わ]いた。
ctx.en: His speech was beautifully structured, and at the end the hall erupted.

ctx.s: 新人賞[しんじんしょう]の選評[せんぴょう]には、「{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}が整[ととの]いすぎて意外性[いがいせい]がない」とあった。
ctx.en: The judges' comments for the newcomer prize said: "The structure is so tidy that there are no surprises."

bad.s: カレーの作[つく]り方[かた]の{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}を教[おし]えてください。
bad.en: (meant: please tell me the steps for making curry)
bad.why: It is the structure of a narrative or text, not the steps of a recipe or procedure. For the steps of a recipe, say tejun.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]、作文[さくぶん]を{起承転結[きしょうてんけつ]}した。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I structured my essay in four parts)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a suru verb. Say kishōtenketsu o ishiki shite kaita.

cards.mean: advancing and falling back by turns
cards.lit: one step forward, one step back

use.how: Said of a situation, not a person's feelings: 病状は一進一退だ, 一進一退の攻防, 一進一退を繰り返す. Implies no clear progress either way.

near.diff: 一喜一憂 is a person's mood swinging with each piece of news; 一進一退 is the situation itself swinging between better and worse.

cards.cue: Your grandmother's condition in hospital improves one day and gets worse the next, with no clear direction.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]の病状[びょうじょう]は{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}だ。
ctx.en: My grandfather's condition keeps getting a little better, then a little worse.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]は最後[さいご]まで{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}の攻防[こうぼう]が続[つづ]いた。
ctx.en: The match was a seesaw battle right to the end.

ctx.s: 「交渉[こうしょう]はどうなってる？」「まだ{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}だね。」
ctx.en: "How are the negotiations going?" "Still one step forward, one step back."

ctx.s: 株価[かぶか]はこの一週間[いっしゅうかん]、{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}を繰[く]り返[かえ]している。
ctx.en: All this week the share price has been going up and down without getting anywhere.

ctx.s: 景気[けいき]は{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}で、本格的[ほんかくてき]な回復[かいふく]にはまだ時間[じかん]がかかりそうだ。
ctx.en: The economy keeps edging forward and slipping back; a full recovery still looks some way off.

ctx.s: 両軍[りょうぐん]は川[かわ]をはさんで、三日間[みっかかん]{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}の戦[たたか]いを続[つづ]けた。
ctx.en: The two armies fought back and forth across the river for three days.

bad.s: 毎日[まいにち]練習[れんしゅう]して、{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}に上手[じょうず]になった。
bad.en: (meant: I practised every day and steadily got better)
bad.why: It means progress and setbacks alternating, not steady step-by-step improvement. Say chakujitsu ni or sukoshi zutsu.

bad.s: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]で{一進一退[いっしんいったい]}しながら彼[かれ]を待[ま]った。
bad.en: (meant: I paced back and forth in front of the station waiting for him)
bad.why: It describes how a situation or contest develops, not physically walking to and fro. Say ittari kitari or urouro.

cards.mean: advancing rapidly day by day, as technology does
cards.lit: advancing every day, striding forward every month

use.how: Said of a field that keeps improving, above all technology, medicine and science: 技術は日進月歩だ, 日進月歩の世界. Not of a single task done quickly.

cards.cue: The laptop you bought three years ago already feels old, because the technology keeps improving so fast.

ctx.s: スマートフォンの技術[ぎじゅつ]は{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}だ。
ctx.en: Smartphone technology improves at a dizzying pace.

ctx.s: 医療[いりょう]は{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}で、昔[むかし]は治[なお]らなかった病気[びょうき]も治[なお]るようになった。
ctx.en: Medicine advances so fast that illnesses that were once incurable can now be treated.

ctx.s: 「このパソコン、もう古[ふる]いの？」「三年前[さんねんまえ]のだからね。{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}の世界[せかい]だよ。」
ctx.en: "This computer's already out of date?" "It's three years old. Things move fast in that world."

ctx.s: {日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}の人工知能[じんこうちのう]の技術[ぎじゅつ]に、法律[ほうりつ]が追[お]いついていない。
ctx.en: The law has not kept up with fast-advancing AI technology.

ctx.s: 研究[けんきゅう]の世界[せかい]は{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}なので、常[つね]に最新[さいしん]の論文[ろんぶん]を読[よ]む必要[ひつよう]がある。
ctx.en: Research moves forward so quickly that you always have to read the latest papers.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]は年頭[ねんとう]のあいさつで、「{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}の時代[じだい]に、変化[へんか]を恐[おそ]れてはならない」と述[の]べた。
ctx.en: In his New Year address the president said: "In an age of constant progress, we must not fear change."

bad.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの準備[じゅんび]は{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}で、一日[いちにち]で終[お]わった。
bad.en: (meant: the moving preparations went very fast and were done in a day)
bad.why: It describes a field improving continually over months and years, not a single job finished quickly.

bad.s: 最近[さいきん]、物価[ぶっか]が{日進月歩[にっしんげっぽ]}で上[あ]がっている。
bad.en: (meant: prices have been rising rapidly lately)
bad.why: It means progress or improvement. Rising prices are not progress; say dondon agatte iru.

cards.mean: great talent takes a long time to mature
cards.lit: a great vessel is finished late

story.text: Chapter 41 of the Daodejing, attributed to Laozi, describes the Way through a string of paradoxes: the great square has no corners, the great vessel is completed late, the great sound is barely heard, the great image has no shape. The line about the vessel, which takes far longer to make than a small cup, became the saying that people of great ability come into their own late.

use.how: Said of a person who succeeds late, or as encouragement to someone not yet successful: 彼は大器晩成だ, 大器晩成の人, 大器晩成型. Not of things or projects.

cards.cue: An actor who struggled unknown for twenty years finally wins a major award in his fifties.

cards.mean: so tense that a clash could erupt at any moment

use.how: 一触即発の状態 / 雰囲気 / 危機, or as a predicate: 一触即発だ. Said of people, groups or countries locked in a standoff that has not exploded yet.

near.diff: 危機一髪 is a narrow escape from a danger that just happened; 一触即発 is a tense standoff before any clash has happened.

cards.cue: Two managers are glaring at each other across the meeting table; one more sharp word and they'll start shouting.

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]はにらみ合[あ]って、{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}の雰囲気[ふんいき]だった。
ctx.en: The two were glaring at each other, and it felt like a fight could break out any second.

ctx.s: 「今[いま]あの二人[ふたり]に話[はな]しかけないほうがいい。{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}だから。」
ctx.en: "Better not talk to those two right now. They're ready to explode."

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]の後[あと]、両[りょう]チームのサポーターが{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}の状態[じょうたい]になった。
ctx.en: After the match, the two teams' supporters were on the verge of clashing.

ctx.s: 遺産[いさん]をめぐって、兄弟[きょうだい]の仲[なか]は{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}だった。
ctx.en: Over the inheritance, things between the brothers were at breaking point.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]が間[あいだ]に入[はい]り、{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}の場[ば]は何[なん]とか収[おさ]まった。
ctx.en: She stepped in between them, and the explosive situation somehow calmed down.

ctx.s: 両国[りょうこく]の対立[たいりつ]は深[ふか]まり、{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}の危機[きき]が続[つづ]いている。
ctx.en: The confrontation between the two countries has deepened, and the danger of open conflict persists.

bad.s: 地震[じしん]で本棚[ほんだな]が倒[たお]れてきて、{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: the bookcase fell over in the earthquake and I only just escaped)
bad.why: For a narrow escape that just happened, say kiki ippatsu. Isshoku sokuhatsu is a tense standoff between opponents.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{一触即発[いっしょくそくはつ]}に怒[おこ]った。
bad.en: (meant: he flew into a rage instantly)
bad.why: It describes a tense situation just before a clash, not how fast someone gets angry, and is not an adverb. Say sugu ni katto natta.

cards.mean: many hardships lie ahead
cards.lit: the road ahead holds many troubles

use.how: 前途多難だ, 前途多難なスタート / 前途多難の船出. Said at the start of a project, team, job or plan when trouble is already in sight.

near.diff: 四苦八苦 is struggling hard right now; 前途多難 forecasts troubles still to come.
Its opposite: 前途洋々 says the future looks bright; 前途多難 says it looks hard.

cards.cue: Your café hasn't even opened yet, and already the budget is short, the chef has quit and the landlord wants to renegotiate. What lies ahead?

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいチームは{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}だ。
ctx.en: The new team has a hard road ahead.

ctx.s: 開店[かいてん]初日[しょにち]から雨[あめ]で、{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}なスタートになった。
ctx.en: It rained from opening day, so it was a rocky start.

ctx.s: 「予算[よさん]も人[ひと]も足[た]りないなんて、{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}だね。」
ctx.en: "Not enough budget and not enough people? There's going to be trouble ahead."

ctx.s: 「英語[えいご]もできないのに留学[りゅうがく]？{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}だけど、応援[おうえん]するよ。」
ctx.en: "Studying abroad when you can't even speak English? It'll be tough, but I'm behind you."

ctx.s: 新監督[しんかんとく]の初戦[しょせん]は大敗[たいはい]に終[お]わり、{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}の船出[ふなで]となった。
ctx.en: The new manager's first match ended in a heavy defeat, a troubled start to the new era.

ctx.s: 町[まち]の復興[ふっこう]は{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}だが、住民[じゅうみん]はあきらめていない。
ctx.en: Rebuilding the town faces many obstacles, but the residents haven't given up.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]の試験[しけん]は{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday's exam was really hard)
bad.why: It looks ahead to troubles still to come. For something already over that was hard, say taihen datta or muzukashikatta.

bad.s: 大学[だいがく]に合格[ごうかく]して、{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}な未来[みらい]が待[ま]っている。
bad.en: (meant: I got into university and a bright future awaits)
bad.why: Tanan means many hardships, so this is the opposite of congratulations. A bright future is zento yōyō.

cards.mean: having a bright and promising future
cards.lit: the road ahead stretches out wide, like a vast open sea

use.how: 前途洋々だ, 前途洋々たる / な / の若者 (たる is the classic written form). Said of young people, graduates, newcomers and new ventures, often in speeches and congratulations.

near.diff: 順風満帆 says things are going smoothly now; 前途洋々 says the future looks bright, often before much has happened.

cards.cue: At the graduation ceremony, the principal looks out at students about to begin their careers, with every door still open to them.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はまだ二十歳[はたち]で、{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}だ。
ctx.en: He's only twenty, with a bright future ahead of him.

ctx.s: 「才能[さいのう]もあるし、まだ若[わか]い。君[きみ]は{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "You're talented and still young. Your future is wide open."

ctx.s: 「{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}な若[わか]いお二人[ふたり]に、乾杯[かんぱい]！」
ctx.en: "A toast to the young couple and the bright future ahead of them!"

ctx.s: 卒業式[そつぎょうしき]で校長[こうちょう]は、{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}の卒業生[そつぎょうせい]たちにエールを送[おく]った。
ctx.en: At the graduation ceremony, the principal cheered on the graduates and their promising futures.

ctx.s: 新人賞[しんじんしょう]を取[と]った彼女[かのじょ]の作家人生[さっかじんせい]は、{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}に見[み]えた。
ctx.en: Having won the newcomer's prize, her career as a writer looked full of promise.

ctx.s: 大[おお]きな契約[けいやく]も決[き]まり、できたばかりの会社[かいしゃ]は{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}だ。
ctx.en: With a big contract signed, the newly founded company has a bright future.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]の旅行[りょこう]は{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}で楽[たの]しかった。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday's trip went smoothly and was fun)
bad.why: It is about the future of a person or venture, not how a past event went. Say junchō de tanoshikatta.

bad.s: 「お子[こ]さんの{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}をお祈[いの]りします。」
bad.en: (meant: I wish your child a bright future)
bad.why: It describes a future; it is not a noun you can wish for. Say o-kosan no go-katsuyaku o o-inori shimasu.

cards.mean: so suspicious that everything seems a threat
cards.lit: a doubting heart sees demons in the dark

story.text: A man lost his axe and suspected his neighbour's son. Watching the boy, he found that his walk, his face and his words all looked like a thief's. Later the man found the axe while digging. The next time he saw the boy, nothing about him looked like a thief at all. A later commentary summed the story up as 'a doubting heart gives rise to demons in the dark', and the phrase comes from that.
story.source: 『列子』説符篇 (the lost axe) and a later commentary on it

use.how: Mostly 疑心暗鬼になる / 疑心暗鬼に陥る, or 疑心暗鬼が広がる. Said of people or groups who, after one doubt, start suspecting everyone and everything.

near.diff: 半信半疑 is half believing one claim; 疑心暗鬼 is suspicion spreading until innocent things look sinister.

cards.cue: After money vanished from the office, everyone started eyeing each other, reading guilt into every late arrival and whisper.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]だまされてから、{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}になっている。
ctx.en: Ever since I was tricked once, I've been suspicious of everything.

ctx.s: 「みんなが私[わたし]の悪口[わるぐち]を言[い]ってる気[き]がする」「それは{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}になってるだけだよ。」
ctx.en: "I feel like everyone's talking behind my back." "You're just being paranoid."

ctx.s: 財布[さいふ]がなくなって以来[いらい]、クラス中[じゅう]が{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}に陥[おちい]った。
ctx.en: Since the wallet went missing, the whole class has been suspicious of one another.

ctx.s: 情報[じょうほう]が少[すく]ないと、人[ひと]は{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}になりやすい。
ctx.en: When information is scarce, people easily start suspecting everything.

ctx.s: 恋人[こいびと]の帰[かえ]りが少[すこ]し遅[おそ]いだけで、{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}になってしまう。
ctx.en: Just because my partner is a little late home, I start imagining the worst.

ctx.s: 社内[しゃない]に{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}が広[ひろ]がり、誰[だれ]も本音[ほんね]を言[い]わなくなった。
ctx.en: Distrust spread through the company, and no one said what they really thought anymore.

bad.s: このニュースが本当[ほんとう]かどうか、{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: I'm not sure whether this news is true)
bad.why: For doubting a single claim, say hanshin hangi. Gishin anki is suspicion grown so large that everything looks like a threat.

bad.s: 店員[てんいん]を{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}して、警察[けいさつ]に連絡[れんらく]した。
bad.en: (meant: I suspected the shop assistant and called the police)
bad.why: It is not a suru verb and takes no object; you gishin anki ni naru. To suspect a person, say ten'in o utagatte.

cards.mean: giving up on oneself in despair
cards.lit: doing violence to oneself and throwing oneself away

story.text: Mencius said that there is no talking with those who do violence to themselves, and no achieving anything with those who throw themselves away. To speak against propriety and righteousness is to do violence to yourself; to say 'I cannot live by benevolence and follow righteousness' is to throw yourself away. The two terms of that saying, jibō and jiki, were joined into this phrase.

use.how: 自暴自棄になる / 自暴自棄な生活, 自暴自棄にならないで. Said of someone who, after a failure or loss, stops caring what becomes of them.

near.diff: 意気消沈 is being downcast; 自暴自棄 goes further: giving up on yourself and acting recklessly against your own good.

cards.cue: After being dumped and fired in the same week, your friend stopped eating properly, drank every night and said nothing mattered anymore.

ctx.s: 失恋[しつれん]して{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}になった。
ctx.en: After the breakup, I stopped caring what happened to me.

ctx.s: 「一回[いっかい]失敗[しっぱい]したくらいで、{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}にならないで。」
ctx.en: "Don't throw it all away over one failure."

ctx.s: 受験[じゅけん]に失敗[しっぱい]した彼[かれ]は、{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}な生活[せいかつ]を送[おく]っていた。
ctx.en: After failing his entrance exams, he was living a reckless, self-destructive life.

ctx.s: 「もうどうなってもいい」と{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}になりかけたとき、友人[ゆうじん]が支[ささ]えてくれた。
ctx.en: Just as I was about to give up on myself, thinking nothing mattered, a friend stood by me.

ctx.s: 小説[しょうせつ]の主人公[しゅじんこう]は、家族[かぞく]を失[うしな]って{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}に陥[おちい]る。
ctx.en: The novel's hero loses his family and sinks into despair.

ctx.s: けがで引退[いんたい]した選手[せんしゅ]が、{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}の日々[ひび]から立[た]ち直[なお]る物語[ものがたり]だ。
ctx.en: It's the story of an athlete forced to retire by injury who recovers from days of self-destruction.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]で遠足[えんそく]が中止[ちゅうし]になり、子[こ]どもたちは{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}になった。
bad.en: (meant: the trip was rained off and the children were disappointed)
bad.why: Far too strong for a small letdown: it means giving up on yourself and your life. Say gakkari shita.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{自暴自棄[じぼうじき]}に勉強[べんきょう]して、合格[ごうかく]した。
bad.en: (meant: he studied desperately hard and passed)
bad.why: It means abandoning yourself, not all-out effort. For desperate effort say hisshi ni or isshōkenmei.

cards.mean: downcast and discouraged
cards.lit: one's spirits fade away and sink

use.how: 意気消沈する / 意気消沈した様子. Said of a person or group who has lost heart after a defeat, a failure or bad news.

near.diff: 自暴自棄 is giving up on yourself and acting recklessly; 意気消沈 is only losing heart, and it usually passes.

cards.cue: The team trained all year, then lost the final in the last second; on the bus home nobody said a word.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]に負[ま]けて、選手[せんしゅ]たちは{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}していた。
ctx.en: Having lost the match, the players were downcast.

ctx.s: 「どうしたの、そんなに{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}した顔[かお]して。」
ctx.en: "What's wrong? You look so crestfallen."

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]に落[お]ちた息子[むすこ]は、{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}して部屋[へや]にこもっている。
ctx.en: My son failed the interview and is shut up in his room, utterly discouraged.

ctx.s: 新商品[しんしょうひん]が全[まった]く売[う]れず、開発[かいはつ]チームは{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}した。
ctx.en: The new product didn't sell at all, and the development team lost heart.

ctx.s: 大敗[たいはい]で{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}するファンを、監督[かんとく]の言葉[ことば]が励[はげ]ました。
ctx.en: The manager's words lifted the spirits of fans dejected by the heavy defeat.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]断[ことわ]られても、彼女[かのじょ]は{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}することなく営業[えいぎょう]を続[つづ]けた。
ctx.en: No matter how often she was turned down, she kept on selling without losing heart.

bad.s: 毎日[まいにち]雨[あめ]で、空[そら]が{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}している。
bad.en: (meant: it rains every day and the sky is gloomy)
bad.why: It describes the spirits of a person or group, not weather or things. For a gloomy sky say don'yori shite iru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は生[う]まれつき{意気消沈[いきしょうちん]}な性格[せいかく]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he has a gloomy personality by nature)
bad.why: It is a temporary loss of heart after a setback, not a character trait, and it takes suru, not na. Say kurai seikaku da.

cards.mean: a life or story full of dramatic ups and downs
cards.lit: waves ten thousand jō high (a jō is about three metres): a sea of huge, surging waves

use.how: Usually 波乱万丈の人生 / 生涯 / 物語, or 人生は波乱万丈だった. Said of a whole life, career or long story full of dramatic highs and lows.

near.diff: 紆余曲折 is the winding course a plan or process takes to an outcome; 波乱万丈 is a dramatic life or story.

cards.cue: Your grandmother survived a shipwreck, built a business, lost it, and remarried at seventy; everyone says her life should be a film.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}の人生[じんせい]を送[おく]った。
ctx.en: My grandmother led a life full of drama.

ctx.s: 「あの俳優[はいゆう]って、{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}な人生[じんせい]だったんだね。」
ctx.en: "So that actor had a really eventful life, huh."

ctx.s: この映画[えいが]は、ある冒険家[ぼうけんか]の{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}の生涯[しょうがい]を描[えが]いている。
ctx.en: This film depicts the dramatic life of an adventurer.

ctx.s: 起業[きぎょう]、倒産[とうさん]、そして再起[さいき]。彼[かれ]の三十代[さんじゅうだい]はまさに{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}だった。
ctx.en: Founding a company, going bankrupt, then bouncing back: his thirties were a real rollercoaster.

ctx.s: 「私[わたし]の人生[じんせい]なんて、{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}とはほど遠[とお]いよ。」
ctx.en: "My life is nowhere near that dramatic."

ctx.s: 自伝[じでん]には、戦後[せんご]を生[い]き抜[ぬ]いた{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}の半生[はんせい]がつづられている。
ctx.en: The autobiography recounts a turbulent life lived through the postwar years.

bad.s: 計画[けいかく]は{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}を経[へ]て、やっと決[き]まった。
bad.en: (meant: after many twists and turns the plan was finally settled)
bad.why: For a plan that reaches a decision by a winding route, say uyo kyokusetsu o hete. Haran banjō is for a dramatic life or story.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}な人[ひと]で、話[はな]すと楽[たの]しい。
bad.en: (meant: he's a colourful, lively person and fun to talk to)
bad.why: It describes a life or story, not a personality. Say haran banjō no jinsei o okutta hito, or omoshiroi hito.

cards.mean: many twists and turns before reaching an outcome
cards.lit: meandering and bending, like a road that keeps winding

use.how: Mostly 紆余曲折を経て + outcome, 紆余曲折の末, or 紆余曲折があった. Said of plans, negotiations, relationships or careers that reached a result by a complicated route.

near.diff: 試行錯誤 is deliberately trying methods until one works; 紆余曲折 is the complicated course events took on their own.
波乱万丈 is a dramatic life or story; 紆余曲折 stresses the winding path to one particular outcome.

cards.cue: The station redevelopment was proposed, cancelled, redesigned twice and held up by lawsuits; ten years later it finally opened.

ctx.s: {紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}を経[へ]て、二人[ふたり]は結婚[けっこん]した。
ctx.en: After many twists and turns, the two of them got married.

ctx.s: 「この企画[きかく]が通[とお]るまで、いろいろ{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}があったんですよ。」
ctx.en: "There were all sorts of ups and downs before this proposal got approved."

ctx.s: 新駅[しんえき]の建設[けんせつ]は、{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}の末[すえ]ようやく実現[じつげん]した。
ctx.en: After a long and winding process, the new station was finally built.

ctx.s: {紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}はあったが、交渉[こうしょう]は最終的[さいしゅうてき]にまとまった。
ctx.en: There were complications, but the negotiations were concluded in the end.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]が教師[きょうし]になるまでには、多[おお]くの{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}があった。
ctx.en: She went through many twists and turns before she became a teacher.

ctx.s: 様々[さまざま]な{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}を乗[の]り越[こ]え、チームは初優勝[はつゆうしょう]を果[は]たした。
ctx.en: Having come through all kinds of twists and turns, the team won its first championship.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}な性格[せいかく]で、付[つ]き合[あ]いにくい。
bad.en: (meant: he has a twisted personality and is hard to get along with)
bad.why: It describes the course events take, not a person's character. For a twisted, difficult person say hinekureta seikaku.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]に向[む]けて、{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}して勉強法[べんきょうほう]を探[さが]した。
bad.en: (meant: I tried various study methods by trial and error before the exam)
bad.why: For deliberately trying methods until one works, say shikō sakugo shite. Uyo kyokusetsu is the winding course events took.

cards.mean: running around busily to get something done
cards.lit: to dash east and run west: rushing from one place to another

use.how: Used with する or as 東奔西走の日々. Said of someone busily going from place to place for a purpose: raising money, preparing an event, finding a solution.

near.diff: 右往左往 is running about in confusion, not knowing what to do; 東奔西走 is purposeful running around to get a job done.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は毎日[まいにち]、仕事[しごと]で{東奔西走[とうほんせいそう]}している。
ctx.en: My father is out rushing around for work every day.

ctx.s: 資金[しきん]を集[あつ]めるために、社長[しゃちょう]は{東奔西走[とうほんせいそう]}した。
ctx.en: The company president ran around everywhere to raise funds.

ctx.s: 結婚式[けっこんしき]の準備[じゅんび]で、ここ数週間[すうしゅうかん]は{東奔西走[とうほんせいそう]}の毎日[まいにち]だった。
ctx.en: With the wedding preparations, the past few weeks have been one long rush from place to place.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]忙[いそが]しそうだね。」「新[あたら]しい店[みせ]の物件探[ぶっけんさが]しで{東奔西走[とうほんせいそう]}しているんだ。」
ctx.en: "You look busy lately." "I'm running all over the place looking for premises for the new shop."

ctx.s: 町[まち]の復興[ふっこう]に向[む]けて、町長[ちょうちょう]は今[いま]も{東奔西走[とうほんせいそう]}を続[つづ]けている。
ctx.en: The mayor is still travelling tirelessly here and there to get the town rebuilt.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]が{東奔西走[とうほんせいそう]}してくれたおかげで、イベントは無事[ぶじ]に開[ひら]かれた。
ctx.en: Thanks to all his running around, the event went ahead without a hitch.

bad.en: (meant: the startled customers ran around in panic looking for the exit)

cards.mean: too early to act yet

bad.en: (meant: the cherry blossoms came out early this year)

cards.mean: a warm and friendly atmosphere

cards.mean: with complete sincerity

cards.mean: everyone uniting to work toward one goal
cards.lit: to agree as one and bind together into a single mass

bad.en: (meant: I buckled down by myself and finished my homework)

cards.mean: agreed unanimously by everyone present

near.diff: 異口同音 is many people saying the same thing; 満場一致 is a meeting reaching one decision with no one against.

cards.mean: people of every age, men and women alike

cards.r: しょうしんしょうめい

bad.en: (meant: he is a famous singer who gets asked for autographs everywhere)
bad.why: Yuumei here means having a name, not being famous. The whole means something hollow that exists only in name.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の話[はなし]は{有名無実[ゆうめいむじつ]}で、全部[ぜんぶ]作[つく]り話[ばなし]だった。
bad.en: (meant: his story was groundless; he made it all up)
bad.why: It is said of a rule, title or system with no real function, not of a false story. Say ne mo ha mo nai hanashi.

cards.mean: good and bad mixed together
cards.lit: jade and ordinary stones jumbled together in one heap

story.text: The Jin-dynasty scholar Ge Hong complained that in his day true and false had been turned upside down and jade and stones were mixed together: people could no longer tell fine writings from worthless ones.
story.source: 葛洪『抱朴子』外篇・尚博

use.how: Xは玉石混交だ / 玉石混交のX: said of a mass of things or people (information, entries, shops, applicants) whose quality ranges from excellent to worthless.

near.diff: 十人十色 says people differ in taste or way of thinking, with no ranking; 玉石混交 says quality varies, some good and some worthless.

cards.cue: You search a health question online and find expert articles side by side with wild nonsense. How would you sum up what is out there?

ctx.s: ネットの情報[じょうほう]は{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}だ。
ctx.en: Information on the internet is a mix of good and bad.

ctx.s: 応募作品[おうぼさくひん]は{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}で、審査[しんさ]に時間[じかん]がかかった。
ctx.en: The entries ranged from excellent to worthless, so judging took a long time.

ctx.s: 「この街[まち]のラーメン屋[や]って、どう？」「{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}だね。当[あ]たりもあるけど。」
ctx.en: "What are the ramen shops in this town like?" "Hit and miss. There are some good ones, though."

ctx.s: 口[くち]コミサイトのレビューは{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}なので、鵜呑[うの]みにしないほうがいい。
ctx.en: Reviews on rating sites are a mixed bag, so you shouldn't take them at face value.

ctx.s: 古本市[ふるほんいち]には{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}の本[ほん]が並[なら]び、掘[ほ]り出[だ]し物[もの]を探[さが]すのが楽[たの]しい。
ctx.en: At the second-hand book fair, gems and junk sit side by side, and hunting for a find is half the fun.

ctx.s: 新規参入[しんきさんにゅう]が相次[あいつ]ぎ、業界[ぎょうかい]は{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}の状態[じょうたい]にある。
ctx.en: With one newcomer after another entering, the industry is now a mix of solid firms and dubious ones.

bad.s: このクラスは国籍[こくせき]が{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}で、国際的[こくさいてき]だ。
bad.en: (meant: this class is international, with students of many nationalities)
bad.why: It sorts things into valuable and worthless, so using it of nationalities insults some of them. For neutral variety say samazama or takokuseki.

bad.s: 「うちのチームは{玉石混交[ぎょくせきこんこう]}で、全員[ぜんいん]が優秀[ゆうしゅう]です。」
bad.en: (meant: our team is diverse and everyone in it is excellent)
bad.why: It says some of the members are worthless, so it contradicts 'everyone is excellent' and can never be praise of a whole group.

cards.mean: innocent, open and unaffected
cards.lit: one's heaven-given true nature, shining out in full bloom

use.how: 天真爛漫な (person, smile, character) or 天真爛漫だ: a person, often a child or young woman, whose natural, unguarded brightness shows freely.

near.diff: 無邪気 is the everyday word for childlike innocence; 天真爛漫 is the more literary compound and stresses a sunny, open nature with no pretence.

cards.cue: A five-year-old at the party chats happily with every stranger and laughs at everything, with no shyness or pretence at all.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもたちの{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}な笑顔[えがお]に癒[いや]された。
ctx.en: The children's carefree, innocent smiles lifted my spirits.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}な性格[せいかく]で、誰[だれ]からも好[す]かれている。
ctx.en: She has an open, guileless nature, and everyone likes her.

ctx.s: 「お嬢[じょう]さん、本当[ほんとう]に{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}ですね。」「ええ、元気[げんき]すぎて大変[たいへん]ですよ。」
ctx.en: "Your daughter is so sunny and natural." "Yes, she has almost too much energy."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は九十歳[きゅうじゅっさい]になった今[いま]も{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}で、よく声[こえ]を出[だ]して笑[わら]う。
ctx.en: Even at ninety, my grandmother is as open-hearted as a child and often laughs out loud.

ctx.s: {天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}な主人公[しゅじんこう]が、重[おも]いテーマの物語[ものがたり]に明[あか]るさを添[そ]えている。
ctx.en: The open-hearted heroine brings some brightness to a story with a heavy theme.

ctx.s: 子犬[こいぬ]のように{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}に駆[か]け回[まわ]る弟[おとうと]を、みんなが笑[わら]って見[み]ていた。
ctx.en: Everyone smiled as they watched my little brother run around, carefree as a puppy.

bad.s: 山[やま]の{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}な景色[けしき]に感動[かんどう]した。
bad.en: (meant: I was moved by the unspoiled mountain scenery)
bad.why: It describes a person's character and manner, not landscapes or things. For untouched nature say tetsukazu no shizen.

bad.s: 弟[おとうと]はいつも{天真爛漫[てんしんらんまん]}している。
bad.en: (meant: my little brother is always innocent and cheerful)
bad.why: It works like a na-adjective and does not take suru: say itsumo tenshin-ranman da, or tenshin-ranman na otouto.

cards.mean: behaving selfishly as if no one else were there
cards.lit: acting as if there were no one beside you

story.text: Before his attempt on the life of the King of Qin, the swordsman Jing Ke lived in the state of Yan and drank every day in the market with a dog butcher and the musician Gao Jianli. When they were drunk, Gao played the zhu and Jing Ke sang along; they laughed, then wept together, as if no one else were there.

use.how: 傍若無人な態度／振る舞い, 傍若無人に振る舞う: criticises loud or selfish behaviour in front of others that ignores them completely.

near.diff: 自分勝手 is any selfishness, even in private choices; 傍若無人 is selfish, rude behaviour done openly in front of others, as if they did not exist.

cards.cue: On a quiet late-night train, a group of passengers shouts, plays music aloud and puts their feet up on the seats, ignoring everyone around them.

ctx.s: 電車[でんしゃ]の中[なか]で、若者[わかもの]たちが周[まわ]りの目[め]も気[き]にせず{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}に騒[さわ]いでいた。
ctx.en: On the train, a group of young people were making a racket, not caring in the least who was watching.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}な態度[たいど]に、周[まわ]りの客[きゃく]はあきれていた。
ctx.en: The other customers were appalled by his total disregard for everyone.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]、列[れつ]に割[わ]り込[こ]んできたよ。」「周[まわ]りの人[ひと]が見[み]えてないのかな。{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}だね。」
ctx.en: "That man just pushed into the queue." "Can't he see anyone around him? He acts as if nobody else exists."

ctx.s: 図書館[としょかん]で{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}に電話[でんわ]をする人[ひと]がいて、集中[しゅうちゅう]できなかった。
ctx.en: Someone was talking on the phone in the library without a thought for anyone, and I couldn't concentrate.

ctx.s: 観光地[かんこうち]での一部[いちぶ]の旅行者[りょこうしゃ]の{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}な振[ふ]る舞[ま]いが問題[もんだい]になっている。
ctx.en: The inconsiderate behaviour of some travellers at tourist spots has become a problem.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の息子[むすこ]というだけで、彼[かれ]は社内[しゃない]で{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}に振[ふ]る舞[ま]っている。
ctx.en: Just because he is the president's son, he behaves around the office as if no one else mattered.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は大勢[おおぜい]の前[まえ]でも{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}に話[はな]せる、頼[たの]もしいリーダーだ。
bad.en: (meant: he is a dependable leader who speaks with confidence even before a crowd)
bad.why: It is criticism of rude disregard for others, never praise for composure. For calm confidence say doudou to.

bad.s: 誰[だれ]もいない部屋[へや]で、{傍若無人[ぼうじゃくぶじん]}に歌[うた]を歌[うた]った。
bad.en: (meant: alone in an empty room, I sang freely)
bad.why: The point is ignoring people who are actually there. With no one around there is no one to be rude to; say omoikiri utatta.

cards.mean: shifting the blame onto someone else
cards.lit: responsibility passed on to another person's shoulders

use.how: (Xに)責任転嫁する / それは責任転嫁だ: criticises refusing to own a failure by pinning it on another person or on circumstances.

near.diff: 自業自得 says someone's trouble is their own fault; 責任転嫁 is refusing to admit such a fault and blaming someone else for it.

cards.cue: Your project failed because you missed the deadline, but in the meeting you insist it was all the design team's fault.

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]のミスを部下[ぶか]のせいにするのは{責任転嫁[せきにんてんか]}だ。

ctx.s: 寝坊[ねぼう]したのを目覚[めざ]まし時計[どけい]のせいにするのは、ただの{責任転嫁[せきにんてんか]}だ。

ctx.s: 「売[う]れないのは営業[えいぎょう]が悪[わる]いからだ。」「{責任転嫁[せきにんてんか]}しないでください。商品[しょうひん]にも問題[もんだい]があります。」

ctx.s: 負[ま]けるたびに審判[しんぱん]のせいにする監督[かんとく]の{責任転嫁[せきにんてんか]}に、選手[せんしゅ]たちもうんざりしている。
ctx.en: Even the players are fed up with the coach, who blames the referee every time they lose.

bad.en: (meant: before leaving the company, I handed my duties over to my successor)
bad.why: Handing over work properly is hikitsugi. Sekinin tenka always means unfairly blaming someone else for a failure.

bad.s: 部下[ぶか]のミスだったが、課長[かちょう]は自分[じぶん]に{責任転嫁[せきにんてんか]}した。
bad.en: (meant: it was a subordinate's mistake, but the section chief took the blame)

cards.mean: mixing work matters with private ones
cards.lit: the public and the private, mixed up into one

use.how: 公私混同する / それは公私混同だ: criticises using work time, money or position for private ends, or letting personal ties sway work decisions.

near.diff: 職権乱用 is abusing the powers of an office, a serious charge; 公私混同 is the broader, everyday failing of letting private matters into work.

bad.en: (meant: I keep my work and personal plans together in one diary)

bad.en: (meant: I've become friends with my colleagues and every day is fun)
bad.why: It is always a fault, never a happy blend. Being friends with colleagues is not koushi kondou unless it bends work decisions.

cards.mean: working without sleep or rest
cards.lit: no sleep, no rest

use.how: Mostly 不眠不休で + verb (働く, 作業する, 看病する): working day and night through an urgent period such as a disaster, an outage or a deadline.

near.diff: 一生懸命 is doing your best at anything; 不眠不休 means literally giving up sleep and rest, usually for an emergency or a deadline.
四六時中 says something goes on all day long, often a habit; 不眠不休 is working hard without stopping to sleep or rest.

ctx.en: If you keep working without sleep or rest, sooner or later you will ruin your health.

bad.en: (meant: lately I have insomnia and can't sleep at all at night)
bad.why: It means choosing to work on without sleep, not being unable to sleep. Insomnia is fuminshou, or simply nemurenai.

bad.s: 昼休[ひるやす]みの十分間[じゅっぷんかん]、{不眠不休[ふみんふきゅう]}で単語[たんご]を覚[おぼ]えた。
bad.en: (meant: I studied vocabulary intensely for ten minutes at lunch)
bad.why: Sleep doesn't come into ten minutes. It is for days and nights given up to an urgent task; for a short burst say shuuchuu shite.

cards.mean: with lightning speed
cards.lit: a flash of lightning and the spark struck from a stone: over in an instant

bad.en: (meant: the city at night was dazzlingly bright)
bad.why: The image is the speed of a flash, not its brightness. It is only said of quick actions.

cards.mean: a chance that comes once in a lifetime
cards.lit: one meeting in a thousand years

story.text: Yuan Hong, a writer of the Jin dynasty, wrote verses in praise of famous ministers of the Three Kingdoms era. In the preface he said that for a wise minister to meet a ruler who truly appreciates him is a happy meeting that comes once in a thousand years. The phrase later came to mean any rare and golden opportunity.
story.source: 袁宏「三国名臣序賛」（『文選』）

near.diff: 一期一会 treasures a meeting with someone because it may never come again; 千載一遇 is a rare opportunity you should seize.

ctx.en: With the favourites losing one after another, a golden opportunity came our team's way.

ctx.en: He let a once-in-a-lifetime chance slip away, and he still regrets it.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]研究[けんきゅう]してきた鳥[とり]を間近[まぢか]で観察[かんさつ]できる、{千載一遇[せんざいいちぐう]}の機会[きかい]に恵[めぐ]まれた。
ctx.en: I was blessed with a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to watch, up close, the bird I had studied for years.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]、{千載一遇[せんざいいちぐう]}の大事故[だいじこ]が起[お]きた。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday there was a once-in-a-century accident)
bad.why: It only names welcome opportunities. An unheard-of disaster is zendai-mimon or mizou.

bad.s: このスーパーは毎週[まいしゅう]{千載一遇[せんざいいちぐう]}のセールをやっている。
bad.en: (meant: this supermarket holds an amazing sale every week)
bad.why: Something that happens every week is the opposite of a once-in-a-thousand-years chance; the sentence contradicts itself.

cards.r: せんせんきょうきょう
cards.mean: nervously dreading what may happen
cards.lit: trembling and trembling, fearing and fearing: the first kanji here means to tremble

story.text: The phrase comes from a poem in the Chinese Book of Songs, whose speaker goes about 'trembling and wary, as if standing at the edge of a deep pool, as if treading on thin ice'. There it meant anxious caution, and the last two characters were different ones meaning wary. Japanese now usually writes it with the kanji for fear and uses it for fearful dread.

use.how: 戦々恐々とする／としている: dreading something that may soon happen (job cuts, a scolding, a price rise); often in news writing, or said with mild humour.

near.diff: 疑心暗鬼 is suspicion that makes you imagine threats everywhere; 戦々恐々 is fear of a real thing you expect may happen.

cards.cue: Everyone in the office knows the boss is going through last month's poor figures today, and no one wants to be the one called in.

ctx.s: 社員[しゃいん]たちはリストラの噂[うわさ]に{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}としている。
ctx.en: The staff are living in fear over rumours of job cuts.

ctx.s: 母[はは]にテストの点数[てんすう]がばれないかと、{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}としていた。
ctx.en: I was in dread that my mother would find out my test score.

ctx.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]、今日[きょう]は機嫌[きげん]が悪[わる]いらしいよ。」「みんな{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}だね。」
ctx.en: "Apparently the department head is in a bad mood today." "Everyone must be on tenterhooks, then."

ctx.s: 値上[ねあ]げが続[つづ]き、次[つぎ]は何[なに]が上[あ]がるのかと消費者[しょうひしゃ]は{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}としている。
ctx.en: With prices rising again and again, consumers are nervously waiting to see what goes up next.

ctx.s: 抜[ぬ]き打[う]ち検査[けんさ]の噂[うわさ]が広[ひろ]まり、どの店舗[てんぽ]も{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}としながら準備[じゅんび]を進[すす]めた。
ctx.en: As word of a surprise inspection spread, every branch got ready in a state of nervous dread.

ctx.s: 締[し]め切[き]りを過[す]ぎた原稿[げんこう]を抱[かか]え、編集者[へんしゅうしゃ]からの電話[でんわ]に{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}としている。
ctx.en: With an overdue manuscript on my hands, I live in dread of a call from my editor.

bad.en: (meant: a dog suddenly barked at me and I jumped)
bad.why: It is the dread of waiting for something to happen, not a sudden fright. For a startle say bikkuri shita.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の旅行[りょこう]が楽[たの]しみで、{戦々恐々[せんせんきょうきょう]}としている。
bad.en: (meant: I'm excited about tomorrow's trip)
bad.why: It is always fear of something unwelcome, never eager anticipation. For excitement say wakuwaku shite iru.

cards.mean: learning new things by studying the old
cards.lit: warm up the old and come to know the new

story.text: Confucius said: 'One who goes back over the old and from it understands the new is fit to be a teacher.' In Japan the line is traditionally read as furuki o tazunete atarashiki o shiru, and the four characters became a favourite motto for schools and companies.

use.how: Used as a noun: 温故知新の精神, まさに温故知新だ. Said approvingly, in speeches and writing, of drawing new ideas from tradition, history or past experience.

cards.cue: A young chef revives forgotten village recipes from a century ago and reinvents them as new dishes for a modern menu.

ctx.s: 古典[こてん]を学[まな]ぶ意味[いみ]は、{温故知新[おんこちしん]}にある。
ctx.en: The point of studying the classics lies in learning the new from the old.

ctx.s: 昔[むかし]の遊[あそ]びを今[いま]の授業[じゅぎょう]に取[と]り入[い]れるのは、まさに{温故知新[おんこちしん]}だ。
ctx.en: Bringing old-time games into today's lessons is a perfect case of finding the new in the old.

ctx.s: 「座右[ざゆう]の銘[めい]は何[なん]ですか。」「{温故知新[おんこちしん]}です。歴史[れきし]から学[まな]ぶことが多[おお]いので。」
ctx.en: "What is your personal motto?" "Learning the new from the old. History teaches me so much."

ctx.s: 江戸時代[えどじだい]の技術[ぎじゅつ]を応用[おうよう]した新製品[しんせいひん]は、{温故知新[おんこちしん]}の好例[こうれい]と言[い]える。

ctx.en: As we mark our hundredth year, we will keep taking on new challenges in the spirit of learning from the past.

ctx.s: 過去[かこ]の失敗例[しっぱいれい]を分析[ぶんせき]して新[あら]たな対策[たいさく]を考[かんが]える。これも{温故知新[おんこちしん]}だ。
ctx.en: Analysing past failures to work out new measures: that, too, is learning the new from the old.

bad.s: 昔[むかし]のアルバムを見[み]て、{温故知新[おんこちしん]}の気分[きぶん]に浸[ひた]った。
bad.en: (meant: looking at an old photo album, I was filled with nostalgia)
bad.why: It is about learning something new from the past, not a nostalgic feeling. For nostalgia say natsukashii kimochi ni natta.

bad.s: 古[ふる]いやり方[かた]は全部[ぜんぶ]捨[す]てて、{温故知新[おんこちしん]}でいこう。
bad.en: (meant: let's throw out all the old ways and start fresh)
bad.why: It values the old as the source of the new, so it cannot mean discarding the past.

cards.mean: fair and square, playing strictly by the rules
cards.lit: orderly and correct, grand and imposing: originally an army's well-ordered banners and ranks

story.text: In The Art of War, Sunzi advises a general not to intercept an enemy whose banners are in perfect order, nor to attack an army whose ranks are drawn up in calm, imposing array. In Japanese the phrase came to mean facing a rival openly and fairly, with no tricks.

use.how: Mostly adverbial: 正々堂々と戦う / 勝負する / 言う; also 正々堂々とした態度. Said of competing or speaking up openly and fairly, with no tricks and nothing hidden.

near.diff: 公明正大 describes fair, impartial handling of decisions or affairs with nothing hidden; 正々堂々 is about competing or confronting someone openly, without tricks.

cards.cue: Before the final, both captains promise there will be no diving, no time-wasting and no dirty tricks. How do they say they will play?

ctx.s: 明日[あした]の試合[しあい]は{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}と戦[たたか]おう。
ctx.en: Let's play tomorrow's match fair and square.

ctx.s: 「ずるい手[て]を使[つか]って勝[か]っても嬉[うれ]しくないよ。{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}と勝負[しょうぶ]しよう。」
ctx.en: "Winning with dirty tricks is no fun. Let's have a fair contest."

ctx.s: 「スポーツマンシップにのっとり、{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}と戦[たたか]うことを誓[ちか]います。」
ctx.en: "In the spirit of sportsmanship, we swear to compete fairly and honourably."

ctx.s: 負[ま]けても言[い]い訳[わけ]をしない彼[かれ]の{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}とした態度[たいど]に、観客[かんきゃく]は拍手[はくしゅ]を送[おく]った。
ctx.en: The crowd applauded his sporting attitude: even in defeat he made no excuses.

ctx.s: 両社[りょうしゃ]は相手[あいて]の悪口[わるくち]を言[い]うのではなく、品質[ひんしつ]で{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}と競[きそ]い合[あ]うべきだ。
ctx.en: Instead of running each other down, the two companies should compete fairly on quality.

bad.s: ケーキを妹[いもうと]と{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}に分[わ]けた。
bad.en: (meant: I shared the cake fairly with my sister)
bad.why: It is about competing or confronting openly without tricks, not dividing things equally, and it does not take ni. Say kouhei ni waketa.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しいスーツを着[き]た父[ちち]は、{正々堂々[せいせいどうどう]}として見[み]えた。
bad.en: (meant: in his new suit my father looked dignified)
bad.why: It confuses the idiom with plain doudou: this one speaks of fair play, not of an imposing look. Say doudou to shite mieta.

cards.mean: a contest fought in earnest, with everything at stake
cards.lit: a match fought with real, sharp swords instead of wooden practice ones

use.how: Xは真剣勝負だ / 真剣勝負の場 / 真剣勝負でいく: said of a contest or a job where everyone gives everything and a mistake really costs.

near.diff: 一発勝負 stresses that there is only one chance; 真剣勝負 stresses total seriousness and real stakes, however long the contest lasts.

cards.cue: A veteran sushi chef says that every single piece served to a customer is a fight with no room for a half-hearted moment. What is each piece to him?

ctx.s: 練習[れんしゅう]だからといって手[て]を抜[ぬ]くな。毎回[まいかい]{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}のつもりでやれ。
ctx.en: Don't slack off just because it's practice. Treat every session as the real fight.

ctx.s: プロの世界[せかい]では、毎日[まいにち]が{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}です。
ctx.en: In the professional world, every day is a fight in earnest.

ctx.s: 「手加減[てかげん]しないでね。」「わかった、{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}でいこう。」
ctx.en: "Don't go easy on me." "All right, let's play for real."

ctx.s: 決勝戦[けっしょうせん]は、両[りょう]チームの意地[いじ]がぶつかり合[あ]う{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}となった。
ctx.en: The final became an all-out contest, with both teams' pride on the line.

ctx.s: 将棋[しょうぎ]のタイトル戦[せん]は、何時間[なんじかん]にも及[およ]ぶ{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}だ。
ctx.en: A shogi title match is a battle fought in deadly earnest that can go on for hours.

ctx.s: 職人[しょくにん]にとって、お客[きゃく]さんに出[だ]す一皿[ひとさら]一皿[ひとさら]が{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}なのだ。
ctx.en: For a craftsman, every single dish served to a customer is a contest fought in deadly earnest.

bad.s: 子[こ]どもたちは公園[こうえん]で{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}に遊[あそ]んでいた。
bad.en: (meant: the children were playing very seriously in the park)
bad.why: It is a noun for a contest, not an adverb meaning 'seriously'. Say shinken ni asonde ita.

bad.s: 来週[らいしゅう]の試験[しけん]は{真剣勝負[しんけんしょうぶ]}だから、一回[いっかい]しか受[う]けられない。
bad.en: (meant: next week's exam is a one-chance affair, so you can only sit it once)
bad.why: It says the contest is in earnest, not that there is only one try; the 'because' makes no sense. For one chance, say ippatsu shoubu.

cards.mean: a single attempt that decides everything
cards.lit: a contest settled by a single shot

use.how: Xは一発勝負だ / 一発勝負の試験 / 本番一発勝負: said of an exam, performance or match where there is no second try.

near.diff: 真剣勝負 stresses total seriousness and real stakes; 一発勝負 stresses that everything rides on one try.

cards.cue: There is no rehearsal and no retake: the singers get one go on live television, and whatever happens is what the audience sees.

ctx.s: 入試[にゅうし]は{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}だから緊張[きんちょう]する。
ctx.en: The entrance exam is a one-shot deal, so I'm nervous.

ctx.s: 「リハーサルはないの？」「ないよ。本番[ほんばん]{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}だ。」
ctx.en: "Isn't there a rehearsal?" "No. We get one shot, live."

ctx.s: トーナメントなので、どの試合[しあい]も負[ま]けたら終[お]わりの{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}だ。

ctx.s: 生放送[なまほうそう]は撮[と]り直[なお]しがきかない{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}の世界[せかい]だ。
ctx.en: Live broadcasting is a world where you can't reshoot: you get one take.

ctx.s: 年[ねん]に一度[いちど]しかない資格試験[しかくしけん]に{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}で挑[いど]むのは、かなりのリスクだ。

ctx.s: 複数回[ふくすうかい]受験[じゅけん]できる制度[せいど]にすれば、{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}の弊害[へいがい]を減[へ]らせるという意見[いけん]もある。
ctx.en: Some argue that letting students sit the exam more than once would reduce the harm of an all-or-nothing test.

bad.en: (meant: it's just a quick try, so if it fails you can try again as often as you like)
bad.why: It means there is only one chance, so it contradicts being able to try again. Say kigaru ni tameseru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{一発勝負[いっぱつしょうぶ]}な性格[せいかく]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is the kind of person who bets everything on one throw)
bad.why: It names an event with one chance, not a personality, and it does not take na. Say ichika bachika ni kakeru taipu da.

cards.mean: two people working closely together as partners
cards.lit: two people, three legs: the three-legged race, where partners tie their inner ankles together and must move in step

use.how: XとYが二人三脚で〜する / 夫婦二人三脚で: said of two partners (a couple, coach and athlete, parent and child) who work toward a goal together over time.

near.diff: 一心同体 says people are united as one in heart and body; 二人三脚 pictures two partners keeping in step as they work toward a goal.

cards.cue: A skater, accepting a medal, thanks the coach who has trained beside her every day for ten years, sharing every setback and every step forward.

ctx.s: 母[はは]と{二人三脚[ににんさんきゃく]}で受験[じゅけん]を乗[の]り越[こ]えた。

ctx.en: My parents run a small bakery, the two of them working side by side.

ctx.s: 「優勝[ゆうしょう]できたのはコーチのおかげです。十年間[じゅうねんかん]、{二人三脚[ににんさんきゃく]}でやってきました。」
ctx.en: "I owe this win to my coach. We've worked together as a pair for ten years."

ctx.s: 創業者[そうぎょうしゃ]の二人[ふたり]が{二人三脚[ににんさんきゃく]}で、会社[かいしゃ]をここまで大[おお]きくしてきた。

bad.en: (meant: the whole class worked together to prepare for the school festival)
